pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Reflection & Refraction

- **Standards — UK (DfE KS3 Physics, 'Light waves'):** "use of ray model to explain imaging in mirrors, the pinhole camera, the refraction of light and action of convex lens in focusing (qualitative); light waves travelling through a vacuum; speed of light; the transmission of light through materials: absorption, diffuse scattering and specular reflection at a surface; use of ray model to explain reflection… the refraction of light and how prisms produce a spectrum of white light (qualitative only)." Law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal), plane-mirror virtual images and ray diagrams, and refraction-as-bending are all UK-anchored at KS3; Snell's law is NOT required (qualitative only).

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS-PS4-2):** "[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-PS4-2]." NGSS treats reflection/absorption/transmission qualitatively at MS and does NOT prescribe the law-of-reflection geometry, plane-mirror ray diagrams, or refraction-bending as distinct performance expectations — so the geometric-optics detail of this topic is UK-led; the US anchor supplies the reflect/absorb/transmit framing only.

- **Operational details:** Two behaviours of a light ray meeting a boundary. REFLECTION: teach the normal FIRST (the perpendicular to the surface at the point of incidence) because every angle is measured from it, not from the surface; establish angle of incidence = angle of reflection empirically with a ray box and protractor before naming the law; distinguish specular (smooth surface, parallel rays stay parallel → clear image) from diffuse (rough surface, rays scatter → no image) so pupils see WHY a mirror images but paper does not. Plane-mirror image: locate the virtual image by extending reflected rays BACK behind the mirror (dashed), same distance behind as the object is in front, upright, same size, laterally inverted. REFRACTION: light changes SPEED when it crosses into a different medium and that speed change is what bends it; rarer→denser (e.g. air→water/glass) it slows and bends TOWARD the normal; denser→rarer (water/glass→air) it speeds up and bends AWAY from the normal; a ray along the normal (0° incidence) does not bend. Anchor to the everyday 'bent/broken pencil in a glass of water' and the apparent-depth of a pool. Keep it qualitative: the DIRECTION of bending and the speed-change cause, not Snell's law.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). At 11–12 pupils can reason with a two-object model (ray + boundary) and measure angles, but abstract 'why' (wave speed in a medium) is still forming. Success looks like: correctly drawing and measuring reflection from the normal, constructing a plane-mirror virtual-image ray diagram, and PREDICTING the direction of bend for air→glass and glass→air including the exit case — not merely reciting 'bends toward the normal'. Watch for the transitional error of overgeneralising the denser-medium rule and forgetting light bends back the other way on the way out.
bestPractices: Teach the NORMAL before any angle: draw the perpendicular at the point of incidence first and insist all angles are measured from it, not from the surface — this single move prevents the most common measurement error.
Establish the law of reflection empirically with a ray box + protractor (angle in = angle out) BEFORE stating it as a rule, so the law is a discovered pattern rather than a memorised fact.
Contrast specular vs diffuse reflection side by side (mirror vs paper, both obey the law locally) so pupils see that 'why a mirror images' is about surface smoothness, not a different law.
Locate the plane-mirror image by extending reflected rays BACKWARD as dashed construction lines to the virtual image — make 'virtual = no light actually there, equal distance behind' explicit.

Frame refraction causally: light SLOWS in a denser medium and the speed change bends it; use the 'car wheels hitting mud at an angle' or marching-band analogy to make the slow-side-lags intuition physical.
Always test BOTH crossings — into the denser medium (bends toward normal) AND back out into the rarer medium (bends away) — so the exit case is rehearsed, not assumed symmetric-away.
Anchor to the bent-pencil-in-water and apparent-depth phenomena, then have pupils trace the actual ray path to explain the illusion, connecting the abstract rule to a seen effect.
Keep it strictly qualitative at this stage (direction of bend + speed-change cause); defer Snell's law and refractive index so the mechanism is secure before the maths.
keyRepresentations: Ray diagram with the NORMAL drawn as a dashed perpendicular — the reference line from which incidence and reflection/refraction angles are measured.
Ray box (single narrow beam) hitting a plane mirror and a glass/perspex block — the canonical hands-on manipulative for both behaviours.
Plane-mirror virtual-image construction: object rays, reflected rays, and dashed rays extended behind the mirror meeting at the upright equal-distance image.
Air→glass→air block diagram showing bend-toward-normal on entry and bend-away-on exit (the parallel-displaced emergent ray).
Specular-vs-diffuse pair: parallel rays reflecting off a smooth surface (stay parallel) vs a rough surface (scatter) — why a mirror images and paper does not.
The bent/broken-pencil-in-a-glass-of-water and apparent-shallower-pool images as the everyday phenomena refraction explains.
commonMisconceptions: Measuring angles from the mirror/surface instead of from the normal — the single most frequent geometric error.
Overgeneralising 'denser medium → bends toward the normal' and forgetting the ray bends AWAY from the normal when it exits into the rarer medium.
Confusing reflection with refraction, or thinking a ray does only one at a boundary (light can partially reflect AND refract at the same surface).
Believing light travels in a curve as it bends, rather than travelling straight in each medium and changing direction abruptly at the boundary.
Thinking the OBJECT (e.g. the pencil) physically bends, rather than the light rays from it bending so the eye is deceived.
Teleological 'the light chooses the fastest/shortest path' reasoning offered as a mechanism instead of the speed-change cause.
Assuming the virtual image in a plane mirror is BEHIND the glass 'on' the mirror, or that it is real light, rather than a construction where rays only appear to come from behind.
Assuming a ray entering along the normal (0°) still bends — it changes speed but not direction.

learn.summary: Qualitative geometric optics for 11–12 year-olds: the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal), plane-mirror virtual images (upright, same size, laterally inverted, equal distance behind), and refraction as a speed-change at a boundary that bends an angled ray toward the normal on entering an optically denser (slower) medium and away on leaving it. Core activities let learners vary an incoming ray and observe how the outgoing ray responds, so the law and the speed-change cause are discovered rather than recited. Snell's law and refractive index are deliberately deferred. Supporting activities cover reference diagrams, checks of the exit-case and normal-measuring pitfalls, and hands-on phenomena (bent pencil, apparent depth).

activities.title: Ray bench: discover the reflection law and the refraction bend
feedback: If a learner measures from the surface instead of the normal, point out that the normal is the perpendicular drawn first at the contact point, and every angle is read from it — re-measure one case both ways to see the difference.

If a learner says the ray leaves the block without bending or bends toward the normal a second time: on exit the ray speeds up (glass/water→air) so it bends AWAY from the normal; for a parallel-sided block the emerging ray is parallel to the ray that went in. Trace the speed change at both boundaries.
If a learner expects the 0° ray to bend: it still changes speed, but with no angle there is no sideways lag, so it goes straight through — the bend needs an angled crossing, not just a denser medium.

To make the slow-side-lags idea physical, picture a line of marching-band members (or a car's pair of wheels) crossing at an angle onto slower ground: the side that reaches the slow medium first is held back, so the whole line swings toward the normal — the same angled speed difference bends the light ray.
If a learner draws a curved path inside the block: light travels in a straight line within each medium and changes direction abruptly only at the boundary (a kink, not a curve).

Confirm the virtual image by noting that no light actually reaches behind the mirror — the dashed rays only show where reflected light appears to come from; the image is upright, the same size, equal distance behind, and laterally inverted.
activities.rationale: Reflection and refraction are angle-and-boundary behaviours that become intuitive when a learner changes the incoming ray and watches the outgoing ray respond, linking the speed change to the direction of bend. Teaching the normal first and testing both the entry and exit crossings directly targets the two commonest errors. A speed readout and a density control make the speed-change→bend cause concrete; these are helpful illustrative mechanisms, not required components.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 programme of study anchors reflection (specular/diffuse, ray model), plane-mirror imaging, and qualitative refraction/prisms at KS3, qualitative only (no Snell's law).
Institute of Physics guidance on teaching reflection and refraction: measure from the normal, specular vs diffuse, and the speed-change cause of bending.

Documented refraction misconceptions: overgeneralising 'denser→toward normal', missing the exit-away case, curved-path thinking, object physically bends, measuring from the surface not the normal, teleological least-time reasoning.
learnerActions: Aim one light ray at a flat mirror and vary the angle of the incoming ray; for several angles, measure both the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection FROM the normal (the dashed perpendicular at the point the ray meets the surface), and record the pairs.
State the pattern you find between the two angles in your own words before being told any rule.

Place an object in front of the mirror, trace at least two rays from the same point on it to the mirror and back, then extend the reflected rays backward (as dashed lines) behind the mirror to locate where they appear to meet; mark this virtual image and check that it is upright, the same size as the object, and the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front — and note that it is laterally inverted (left and right swapped).

Swap the mirror for a rectangular (parallel-sided) glass block or water tank. Send the ray in at an angle and describe which way it bends on entering (toward or away from the normal) and which way it bends on leaving the far side.
Set the ray to travel exactly along the normal (0° incidence) and observe whether it changes direction; then tilt it by a small amount and observe again.
If the activity provides a speed indicator, note how the ray's speed changes inside the denser medium and relate that change to whether and which way the ray bends.

If a medium control is available (air → water → glass), switch to an optically denser medium (one where light travels more slowly) and, keeping the same angle of incidence, describe what happens to the size of the bend.
activities.intendedInsight: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection when both are measured from the normal; and a ray bends because it changes speed at a boundary — slowing (air→glass/water) bends it toward the normal, speeding up (glass/water→air) bends it away, while a ray along the normal changes speed but not direction.

activities.title: Why a mirror images but paper does not: specular vs diffuse
feedback: If a learner thinks paper 'breaks the law of reflection', show that at each tiny patch angle in still equals angle out; it is the many differently-tilted patches that scatter the rays.
If a learner cannot explain why a mirror images, point back to the parallel rays staying parallel so the eye can reconstruct a single image.

A sorting task can help check that a learner classifies surfaces correctly, but it does not by itself show the ray behaviour — pair it with observing or sketching the parallel-vs-scatter rays so the reason, not just the category, is understood.
activities.rationale: Contrasting specular and diffuse reflection side by side explains why some surfaces image and others do not, and it reinforces that the law of reflection holds in both cases. This directly addresses a conceptual gap in the KS3 'absorption, diffuse scattering and specular reflection' framing.
sourceClaims: DfE KS3 programme of study anchors reflection (specular/diffuse, ray model), plane-mirror imaging, and qualitative refraction/prisms at KS3, qualitative only (no Snell's law).
Institute of Physics guidance on teaching reflection and refraction: measure from the normal, specular vs diffuse, and the speed-change cause of bending.
learnerActions: Shine a bundle of parallel rays at a smooth surface (mirror) and at a rough surface (paper); observe and sketch what happens to the rays in each case.
Note that on the smooth surface the parallel rays stay parallel after reflecting, while on the rough surface they scatter in many directions.
Check that each individual ray still obeys angle in = angle out from the local normal, even on the rough surface — the difference is that the rough surface tilts the normal differently at each point.
Sort a set of surfaces (polished metal, still water, paper, matte wall, etc.) into those that form a clear image and those that do not, and explain your sorting using the parallel-vs-scatter idea.
activities.intendedInsight: A mirror forms a clear image because its smooth surface keeps reflected rays parallel (specular reflection); a rough surface scatters rays (diffuse reflection) so no image forms — but both obey the law of reflection locally, so the difference is surface smoothness, not a different law.

activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: the reappearing coin and the bent pencil
feedback: If a learner says the pencil or coin physically bends or moves, redirect: the solid object is unchanged; the light rays from it bend at the surface so the eye traces them back to a shifted apparent position.
If a learner predicts no change in the coin view, prompt them to consider that water bends the rising rays so the coin can become visible even though your eye and the coin have not moved.

For the straight-on probe: a 0° ray changes speed but not direction. For the mirror probe: no real light is behind the glass; the image is where rays only appear to originate, so it cannot be caught on a screen. For the denser-material probe: at a given angle, a denser (slower) medium generally bends the ray more — though this depends on the relative speeds of the two media.
activities.rationale: Anchoring the abstract rule to the bent-pencil and apparent-depth phenomena, then having learners trace the actual ray path, connects the mechanism to a seen effect and confronts the 'object physically bends' misconception. The predict-first structure surfaces prior beliefs before observation.
sourceClaims: Documented refraction misconceptions: overgeneralising 'denser→toward normal', missing the exit-away case, curved-path thinking, object physically bends, measuring from the surface not the normal, teleological least-time reasoning.
DfE KS3 programme of study anchors reflection (specular/diffuse, ray model), plane-mirror imaging, and qualitative refraction/prisms at KS3, qualitative only (no Snell's law).
learnerActions: Place a coin at the bottom of an opaque mug, then move your head until the coin is just hidden behind the rim, and keep your head still from then on.
Predict what will happen to your view of the coin as a friend slowly pours water into the mug, and write down WHY before anything is poured.
Pour the water (keeping your head still) and record what you actually saw.
Draw the path of a light ray from the coin, through the water surface, to your eye — showing where it bends and which way — to explain the illusion.
Repeat the reasoning for a pencil standing in a glass of water that looks bent or broken at the surface: explain that it is the light rays that bend, not the pencil.
Discuss the probe questions: would a straight-on (0°) ray change direction? Is there really light behind a mirror where the image appears? Would a much denser material bend the ray more?
activities.intendedInsight: Refraction at the water surface bends light from the coin/pencil so it appears to come from a different place; the object itself does not move or bend — the eye is deceived by the bent rays, and tracing the ray path explains everyday illusions like apparent depth.

activities.title: Two-tier diagnostic: both boundaries of one ray
feedback: Correct full response: bends toward the normal on entry (slowing, air→glass) and away on exit (speeding up, glass→air), with the emergent ray parallel to the incident ray for a parallel-sided block, both bends caused by the speed change at the boundary.

Gap response (bends both boundaries the same way, forgets the exit bend, measures from the surface, or confuses reflection with refraction): rehearse the exit case explicitly and re-establish measuring from the normal.

Partial response (bends toward the normal entering but mishandles the exit, or recites the reflection law without applying the speed-change reason): focus on tracing the speed change at the second boundary.
For the 'glass into air' question, the correct answer is AWAY from the normal; if a learner picks 'toward the normal', revisit which way speed changes on leaving the glass.

If a learner thinks a ray can only reflect OR refract at a surface: a boundary can do both at once — some light reflects (angle in = angle out) while some refracts (passes through and changes direction); these are different behaviours, not alternatives.
activities.rationale: Asking about both boundaries of one ray forces reliance on the speed-change mechanism rather than a single memorised 'denser→toward normal' rule, discriminating full understanding from partial. This is a check of the exit-case and normal-measuring pitfalls, not a substitute for the hands-on ray-bench that builds the causal intuition.
sourceClaims: Documented refraction misconceptions: overgeneralising 'denser→toward normal', missing the exit-away case, curved-path thinking, object physically bends, measuring from the surface not the normal, teleological least-time reasoning.
learnerActions: Consider a ray of light that goes from air INTO a glass block, travels through it, and comes back OUT into the air on the far side.
Describe how the ray bends at EACH boundary — going in and coming out — and state whether it bends toward or away from the normal in each case.
Explain WHY it bends at each boundary in terms of the speed change.
Answer a direction question: a ray goes from glass into air — which way does it bend? (Watch the tempting but wrong 'toward the normal' answer.)
Trace the full path of the ray through a rectangular (parallel-sided) air→glass→air block, including the exit bend, and show that the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray.
activities.intendedInsight: Which way a ray bends depends on whether it speeds up or slows down at that particular boundary — so a single angled ray bends toward the normal entering the glass and away on leaving, emerging parallel to the incident ray for a parallel-sided block; this cannot be answered by one memorised rule applied to both boundaries.

activities.title: Labelled ray diagram as a reference and vocabulary primer
feedback: If a learner confuses the angle of incidence with the angle from the surface, point to the normal callout and re-state that angles are read from the perpendicular.
Use the diagram to settle naming disputes, but encourage learners to then test the behaviour themselves by varying a ray.
activities.rationale: A fixed, well-labelled diagram is an effective vocabulary and reference tool that complements the investigations; it cannot let the learner vary the angle and watch the law hold, so it works best as a companion rather than the sole means of teaching the causal mechanism.
sourceClaims: Institute of Physics guidance on teaching reflection and refraction: measure from the normal, specular vs diffuse, and the speed-change cause of bending.
learnerActions: Study a labelled ray diagram showing a ray reflecting off a mirror and refracting through a block, with the normal, angle of incidence, angle of reflection, angle of refraction, virtual image, and specular/diffuse insets marked.
Reveal and read each callout: the normal is the perpendicular from which every angle is measured; the emergent ray is bent away from the normal because it speeds up leaving the glass.
Use the diagram to name parts and recall vocabulary before or alongside the hands-on ray-bench work.
activities.intendedInsight: A clear reference diagram fixes the vocabulary — normal, incidence, reflection, refraction, virtual image, specular/diffuse — and shows the canonical ray paths, supporting the active investigations.

constraints: Keep the treatment strictly qualitative at this stage: direction of bend and the speed-change cause only. Defer Snell's law and refractive index until the mechanism is secure.
Teach the normal before any angle, and insist all angles are measured from it rather than from the surface.
Always test BOTH crossings — into the denser medium (toward the normal) and back out into the rarer medium (away from the normal) — so the exit case is rehearsed, not assumed.
Note that a single boundary can both reflect and refract at once; reflection and refraction are distinct co-occurring behaviours, not mutually exclusive outcomes.

A labelled static diagram is a scaffold for vocabulary and reference; it does not let learners vary the angle and observe the law holding, so it should accompany, not replace, the hands-on investigation.

A fixed-answer check (direction questions, categorisation, path-tracing with graded responses) verifies that the exit-case and normal-measuring pitfalls are cleared, but does not by itself build the causal intuition; use it alongside active ray work.

Speed readouts, density/medium sliders, live protractors and draggable rays are helpful ways to make the speed-change→bend link concrete, but are optional illustrative mechanisms rather than mandatory features.
Illustrations in checks should be evocative only; do not require learners to read exact angles off a drawn figure.

A 3D scene is not needed for the core planar ray-diagram work; if used at all, reserve it for a peripheral extension such as apparent depth viewed from different angles, and do not render the flat angle-measurement diagram in 3D.
An in-role dialogue (e.g. with an optician or physicist) may motivate interest but, on its own, does not elicit or verify the drawing, measuring and predicting that demonstrate mastery here.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Three details from the original pedagogy were restored because they were lost in an earlier draft: the slow-side-lags refraction analogy (marching band / car wheels crossing onto slower ground), the full plane-mirror image properties (upright, same size, equal distance behind, laterally inverted), and that a boundary can both reflect and refract at once. These come from the original row and were not independently re-verified.

The legacy row's recommendation framed a 2D interactive simulation as uniquely able to make the cause 'felt' and asserted that a quiz 'cannot build the causal intuition', that a dialogue 'cannot deliver' the insight, and that '3D adds nothing'. These comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources; they have been softened to scoped affordances/limits.

The legacy claim that explicit exit-bend and specular/diffuse toggles 'directly attack' the two commonest misconceptions is retained only as a design rationale, not as evidence of effectiveness; no efficacy data is cited.

The interactive-simulation source ('buildable and effective for this concept') is verified:false and contains an unverified efficacy term; it has been removed from the activity sourceClaims because it asserts a medium's effectiveness rather than the teaching principle. The underlying point — that such an interactive is buildable — is noted here only, with efficacy unconfirmed.

Source rows marked verified:false (NGSS MS-PS4-2 framing, the refraction-misconceptions reference, and the simulation claim) carry legacy, unverified status; the standards-alignment and misconception lists are reproduced as provided and should be confirmed against the primary documents.

Self-audit of physics content: entry into a denser (slower) medium bends toward the normal; exit into a rarer (faster) medium bends away; the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray; a 0° ray changes speed but not direction; light travels straight within each medium and kinks only at the boundary. These are consistent across the pedagogy, assessment and learn fields.

The 'denser material bends more on entry' guidance is a reasonable qualitative generalisation for typical media at a given incidence angle but depends on the relative speeds; kept qualitative and not over-claimed.

assess.poeTask: Place a coin at the bottom of an opaque mug, just out of sight below the rim so you can't see it. Predict what happens to your view of the coin when a friend slowly pours water into the mug while you keep still. Say why first, then pour and explain what you saw.
probeDeeper: If the ray hit the glass surface exactly along the normal (straight on, 0 degrees), would it change direction at all? Does its speed still change?
Where is the image in a plane mirror — is there really light behind the glass, or does it just look like it? How could you check?
If the block were made of a much denser material like diamond, would the ray bend more or less on the way in?
assess.correctAnswer: Entering the glass (air to glass, a denser, slower medium) the ray bends TOWARD the normal; leaving the glass (glass to air, faster) it bends AWAY from the normal, so it emerges parallel to the way it came in. The bending happens because the light changes speed as it crosses each boundary.

errorPatterns.pattern: Mishandles the exit: 'it bends toward the normal going in, then comes straight out (or bends the same way again)'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Always rehearse the exit case — glass to air speeds up, so it bends AWAY from the normal; the emergent ray is parallel to the incident one. Trace the speed change both ways.
errorPatterns.distractor: It bends toward the normal going in, and comes straight out without bending.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws or says the exit ray unbent, or bent toward the normal a second time

errorPatterns.pattern: Measures angles from the surface, not the normal
errorPatterns.nextMove: The normal (perpendicular to the surface) is the reference for EVERY angle — draw it first, then measure from it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Measures or marks the angle between the ray and the glass surface rather than the normal

errorPatterns.pattern: Reflection/refraction conflated: treats bending-through as bouncing-back
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reflection = bounces off (angle in = angle out); refraction = passes through and changes direction; a boundary can do both at once.
errorPatterns.distractor: The light bounces back off the glass at the same angle (reflection).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes the refracted ray as reflecting off the glass, or the reflected ray as passing through

errorPatterns.pattern: Curved-path thinking: the ray follows a curve inside the glass
errorPatterns.nextMove: Light travels straight within each medium; it changes direction only AT the boundary (a kink), never a curve.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws a curved ray within the block

errorPatterns.pattern: Virtual image is real light behind the mirror/glass
errorPatterns.nextMove: A virtual image is where the rays only APPEAR to come from (extended back, dashed) — no light is actually there, so you can't catch it on a screen.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says there is real light where a mirror image appears behind the glass

responseLevels.gap: Bends both boundaries the same way or forgets the exit bend, measures angles from the surface, or conflates reflection with refraction.
responseLevels.full: Bends toward the normal entering and away on exiting (emergent ray parallel), attributes both to the speed change at the boundary, measures from the normal, and distinguishes real from virtual images — transferring to the 0-degree and denser-material cases.
responseLevels.partial: Correctly bends the ray toward the normal entering a denser medium (the memorised rule), but mishandles the exit, or can state the law of reflection without applying the speed-change reason to direction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A ray of light goes from air INTO a glass block, travels through it, and comes back OUT into the air on the other side. Describe how the ray bends at EACH boundary — going in, and coming out — and explain why it bends.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Many students learn 'into denser = bend toward the normal' and stop there, so they bend both boundaries the same way or forget the ray bends back on exit. Asking about BOTH boundaries of one ray forces the speed-change mechanism — which way it bends depends on speeding up versus slowing down — rather than a single memorised rule.
